newsitem.title: CANADA: Grain and oilseed prices seen down in 97/98-Ag Can.
newsitem.headline: Grain and oilseed prices seen down in 97/98-Ag Can.

text.p: Canadian wheat, coarse grain and oilseed prices were forecast to decline in crop year 1997/98 (Aug/July) because of larger world output, Agriculture Canada said in its February supply and disposition report.
"Canadian wheat, coarse grain and oilseed prices are expected to decrease in 1997/98 due to increased world production but should remain well above the levels of the early nineties," Ag Canada said.
Price factors include the level of European Union export subsidies, Chinese wheat import needs, the state of the 1997 U.S. winter wheat crop and Brazil's soybean crop.

World wheat and coarse grain prices remained stabled since December 1996 as Argentina sustained excess harvest-time rain that downgraded quantity and quality as well as new import demand from India and Iraq.
U.S. Agriculture Department on Jan 10 lowered the 1997 winter wheat seeded area estimate by seven percent.
The EU's use of export subsidies have been measured and the U.S. has yet to reinstitute its Export Enhancement Program, Ag Canada said.
Canadian wheat, excluding durum, 1996/97 ending stocks were forecast to rise 54 percent to 7.1 million tonnes.
Milling wheat prices were forecast to fall in the C$195 to C$215 a tonne, in-store Vancouver or St. Lawrence in the current crop year, Ag Canada said.
Wheat prices in the coming crop year were expected to slip to C$160 to C$190 a tonne, Ag Canada added.

Durum wheat 1996/97 ending stocks, however, were expected to remain virtually unchanged from the previous year at 2.0 million tonnes with prices in this year forecast at C$208 to C$228 and lower next year at C$185 to C$215 a tonne.
Barley carry-out was raised and exports reduced from the December report due to lower than expected exports to date.
The higher carry-in for 1997/98 should likely offset in part the expected decline in output and slight drop in export.
Barley prices should range from C$125 to C$145 in the current year and C$110 to C$140 next year, Ag Canada said.
Canola crushing in Canada is on track to match last year's record level despite low crushing profit margins.
Lower supplies should keep prices firm and ration exports with 1996/97 carry-out expected to be at "pipeline" levels at about 505,000 tonnes.
Canola's fundamentals should result in more seeded acreage and a decline in prices to the C$390 to C$430 range.
